blocks.title: By the end of the examination, you should be able to:

items.text: Identify diabetic foot ulcers, wounds, calluses, and signs of infection.
Assess peripheral neuropathy, especially loss of protective sensation.
Assess peripheral arterial circulation.
Identify deformities and pressure points that predispose to ulceration.
Recognize a potentially infected foot, critical limb ischaemia, or acute Charcot neuroarthropathy.
Assess the patient's risk of future ulceration and explain preventive measures.
Present your findings clearly to an examiner.

blocks.text: Three major processes explain most diabetic foot complications.
A. Peripheral neuropathy

Damage to sensory nerves causes loss of protective sensation. The patient may develop an ulcer from repetitive pressure, friction, or a foreign body without feeling pain. Motor neuropathy can cause deformities, while autonomic neuropathy may cause dry, cracked skin.
B. Peripheral arterial disease (PAD)

Reduced blood supply impairs tissue healing and increases the risk of necrosis and gangrene. Findings may include weak pulses, cool skin, delayed capillary refill and tissue loss, although no single finding excludes PAD.
C. Repetitive pressure and tissue injury

Loss of sensation, deformity and unsuitable footwear lead to excessive pressure at specific points. Calluses, haemorrhage beneath a callus and ulcers may develop, especially beneath the metatarsal heads and at the heel.

Important clinical principle: Neuropathy and ischaemia frequently coexist. A patient may have a painless, infected ulcer with poor healing, so absence of pain must never reassure you that the foot is healthy.

items.text: Examination couch and adequate lighting.
Disposable gloves if a wound or ulcer is present.
A 10-g Semmes–Weinstein monofilament.
A 128-Hz tuning fork for vibration sensation.
A reflex hammer.
A disposable neurotip or other appropriate sensory-testing instrument.
A handheld Doppler device, if available.
A ruler for measuring an ulcer.
A clean dressing and appropriate wound-assessment supplies if required.

blocks.text: A suitable OSCE introduction is:

“Good morning. My name is … I have been asked to examine your feet because diabetes can affect the nerves and circulation. I will need to inspect both feet, test sensation, assess the blood supply and examine for any wounds or deformities. Some parts may involve light touch or gentle pressure. Please tell me if you experience any discomfort. Is that alright?”

items.text: Confirm the patient's identity.
Explain the procedure and obtain consent.
Ask about pain before touching the feet.
Ask permission to expose both feet and lower legs.
Provide privacy and adequate lighting.
Position the patient comfortably, usually lying supine or sitting with both feet accessible.
Wash your hands and use gloves when indicated.
Ensure both feet are examined and compare them throughout.

blocks.text: OSCE tip: Never examine only the foot with the visible ulcer. Bilateral examination helps identify asymmetry, contralateral risk factors and unrecognized disease.
Use this sequence:
1. General assessment
Patient's general condition, diabetes history and risk factors
2. Inspection
Skin, nails, ulcers, infection and deformities
3. Neurological assessment
Protective sensation, vibration and reflexes
4. Vascular assessment
Temperature, capillary refill, pulses and Doppler when indicated
5. Deformities and footwear
Pressure points, mobility, gait and shoe assessment
Before examining the feet, ask targeted questions and observe the patient.

items.text: Duration and control of diabetes.
Previous foot ulcers, amputations or foot surgery.
Numbness, tingling, burning or loss of sensation.
Foot pain, especially pain on walking or pain at rest.
Previous wounds, blisters, burns or unnoticed injuries.
Wound duration, discharge, odour and progression.
Fever, chills or feeling generally unwell.
Smoking, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and kidney disease.
Footwear, barefoot walking and routine foot care.
Difficulty walking or transferring.
Walking aids or protective footwear.
Evidence of previous toe or limb amputation.
A dressing, offloading boot or walking cast.
Systemic illness if an infected foot is suspected.

blocks.text: **Interpretation**

rows: Advanced ischaemia, particularly if persistent and relieved by dependency

blocks.text: A normal history does not exclude neuropathy or PAD. Some patients are unaware of their disease.
Expose both feet fully, including the soles, heels, interdigital spaces and ankles. Inspect the feet first without touching them.
**A. Skin colour and condition**

items.text: Normal pigmentation versus pallor, cyanosis or dependent rubor.
Dryness, fissures and cracks.
Scaling or maceration between the toes.
Calluses and corns.
Blisters and pressure marks.
Localised swelling or redness.
Shiny, thin skin or loss of hair, which may accompany arterial disease.

blocks.text: Normal finding: Skin is intact, with no concerning colour changes, fissures, calluses, maceration or pressure lesions.

items.text: Dry, cracked skin: may reflect autonomic neuropathy and increases the risk of entry of infection.
Thick callus: repeated pressure or friction; haemorrhage beneath it may indicate impending ulceration.
Pallor or dependent rubor: may indicate arterial insufficiency.
Interdigital maceration: moisture damage, sometimes associated with fungal infection.
Redness and warmth: consider infection, inflammation or acute Charcot neuroarthropathy.

blocks.text: Do not diagnose PAD from shiny skin or absent hair alone; these findings are nonspecific.
**B. Nails and interdigital spaces**

items.text: Thickened or deformed nails.
Fungal nail infection.
Ingrown nails.
Nail-bed injury.
Ulcers or fissures between the toes.
Maceration and fungal skin disease.

blocks.text: These abnormalities may create pressure injury or provide a portal for infection.
OSCE statement: “The nails and interdigital spaces are normal, with no evidence of fungal disease, maceration, fissures or nail trauma.”
**C. Ulcer assessment**
If an ulcer is present, describe it systematically.
1. Site
Plantar surface, heel, toe tips, interdigital spaces, dorsum or margins of the foot. Plantar pressure points often suggest a neuropathic component.
2. Size and shape
Measure length and width in centimetres; document depth if safely assessable. Record whether the lesion is superficial, crater-like or deep.
3. Wound bed and margins
Describe granulation tissue, slough, necrosis, callus, undermining and the condition of the edges.
4. Infection and tissue viability
Look for purulent discharge, spreading redness, warmth, swelling, necrosis, gangrene, exposed tendon or bone, and any associated odour.
Also document surrounding callus, undermining, foreign bodies if visible, and whether there are multiple ulcers.

items.text: Do not aggressively debride a callus during a routine examination.
Do not probe deeply or attempt to expose bone without appropriate training and clinical indication.
A probe-to-bone test may be useful in a clinically indicated assessment by a trained clinician, but a negative result does not exclude osteomyelitis.
Do not assume that an ulcer is uninfected simply because there is no pus or fever.

blocks.text: **Common ulcer patterns**

rows: Plantar pressure points, metatarsal heads, heel
May be painful; pain can be absent if neuropathy coexists
May be cool, pale or show dependent rubor
Frequently poor because of reduced perfusion

blocks.text: These are typical patterns, not absolute rules. Mixed neuropathic-ischaemic ulcers are common.
**Step 3: Neurological examination**
The most important purpose is to detect loss of protective sensation (LOPS), which allows repetitive injury to progress unnoticed.
**A. Ten-gram monofilament test**
This tests protective pressure sensation.
practice.dm-rg.net
Use a validated 10-g monofilament and the appropriate guideline-specific testing sites.

items.text: Explain the test and demonstrate it on the patient's hand or forearm.
Ask the patient to close their eyes.
Ensure the foot is relaxed.
Avoid testing directly over an ulcer, thick callus, scar or necrotic area.
Apply the monofilament perpendicular to the skin until it bends, using a controlled, brief contact of approximately one second.
Lift it away; do not slide it across the skin.
Randomly apply the filament at the recommended plantar sites, asking the patient to say when they feel it.
Include occasional sham applications if appropriate, to assess response reliability.
Record each site as perceived or not perceived and compare both feet.

blocks.text: A commonly used approach assesses the plantar surface of the hallux and the first, third and fifth metatarsal heads, but follow the validated protocol required by your examination or local guideline.
Normal finding: The patient correctly perceives the monofilament at all required sites.
Abnormal finding: Failure to perceive the stimulus at one or more required sites suggests impaired protective sensation and increased ulcer risk.

items.text: Letting the patient watch the examination.
Applying the filament too briefly or with insufficient force.
Dragging the filament over the skin.
Testing over calluses or ulcers.
Asking leading questions that influence the patient's answers.

blocks.text: **B. Vibration sense — 128-Hz tuning fork**
This assesses large-fibre sensory function.

items.text: Strike the tuning fork gently to produce vibration.
Place its base on a bony prominence, commonly the distal interphalangeal joint of the great toe.
Ask the patient to report when vibration begins and when it stops.
Compare with your own perception if needed.
If absent at the toe, test at a more proximal site such as the malleolus.

blocks.text: Normal finding: Vibration is perceived and its cessation is correctly identified.
Abnormal finding: Reduced or absent vibration suggests large-fibre peripheral neuropathy.
**C. Pinprick sensation**
Use an appropriate disposable neurotip to compare sharp and blunt sensations, asking the patient to identify the stimulus with their eyes closed.

items.text: Normal: correctly distinguishes sharp from blunt at the tested sites.
Abnormal: reduced or absent pinprick sensation suggests sensory dysfunction.

blocks.text: Avoid breaking the skin.
**D. Temperature sensation**
If indicated, assess the ability to distinguish safe warm and cool stimuli using an appropriate clinical instrument.

items.text: Normal: correctly identifies warm and cool.
Abnormal: impaired temperature sensation may indicate small-fibre dysfunction.

blocks.text: Never use hot objects or extreme temperatures on an insensate foot.
**E. Ankle reflexes**
Test the Achilles tendon reflex.

items.text: Position the foot so the ankle is slightly dorsiflexed.
Strike the Achilles tendon with a reflex hammer.
Observe plantar flexion.
Compare both sides.

blocks.text: Normal: Reflexes are present and reasonably symmetrical, allowing for age and clinical context.
Abnormal: Reduced or absent ankle reflexes may support a diagnosis of peripheral neuropathy, but they are not diagnostic on their own.
**F. Motor function and deformity**
Assess toe movement and ankle dorsiflexion and plantar flexion. Look for intrinsic muscle wasting and clawing of the toes.
Weakness and muscle imbalance may contribute to deformities and abnormal plantar pressure.

High-yield distinction: The monofilament detects loss of protective pressure sensation; the tuning fork assesses vibration. They test related but different sensory functions, so one does not fully replace the other.
**Step 4: Vascular examination**
The aim is to identify peripheral arterial disease and determine whether tissue perfusion may be inadequate for wound healing.
**A. Temperature**
Use the backs of your fingers to compare corresponding areas of both feet, moving from the lower leg towards the toes.

items.text: Normal: Feet are reasonably warm and symmetrical.
Abnormal: A persistently cool foot, especially with weak pulses, pallor or tissue loss, raises suspicion of arterial insufficiency.
Important exception: An acutely inflamed or infected foot, or a foot affected by Charcot neuroarthropathy, may be warm despite coexisting arterial disease.

blocks.text: **B. Capillary refill time**
Press the toe pulp or nail bed until it blanches, then release and observe colour return.

items.text: Normal: Prompt return of colour, commonly within about two seconds in a warm, adequately perfused foot.
Abnormal: Delayed refill may suggest impaired perfusion, but it is affected by ambient temperature, age and other factors.

blocks.text: Capillary refill alone cannot diagnose or exclude PAD.
**C. Peripheral pulses**
You must identify and assess both the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses.
1. Dorsalis pedis artery
Palpate on the dorsum of the foot, usually just lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus. Use the pads of your index and middle fingers, not your thumb.
2. Posterior tibial artery
Palpate behind and slightly below the medial malleolus, between the malleolus and the Achilles tendon.
Assess each pulse bilaterally and document its presence, strength and symmetry.

items.text: 0: absent.
1+: weak or diminished.
2+: normal.
3+: bounding.

blocks.text: Normal finding: Both dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable bilaterally, with no significant asymmetry.
Abnormal finding: A weak or absent pulse increases suspicion of PAD. However, an absent dorsalis pedis pulse can occur in some healthy individuals, and palpable pulses do not exclude PAD.
**D. Handheld Doppler assessment**
If pulses are difficult to palpate or PAD is suspected, Doppler assessment may be necessary.

items.text: Audible arterial flow and waveform characteristics help assess perfusion.
A multiphasic waveform is generally more reassuring than a monophasic waveform.
A monophasic waveform suggests arterial disease.
An absent Doppler signal is concerning and warrants urgent clinical assessment.

blocks.text: Interpret Doppler findings alongside symptoms, examination, and objective vascular testing.
**E. Ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI)**
ABPI is an investigation rather than a purely physical examination manoeuvre, but it is important to understand for OSCE questions.
Use the appropriate standard measurement protocol for ankle and brachial pressures.

Crucial diabetic-foot point: Medial arterial calcification may make arteries poorly compressible, producing a falsely normal or elevated ABPI. When PAD remains suspected, toe pressure/toe-brachial index, Doppler waveforms or other vascular investigations may be more informative.
Do not rely on ABPI alone to exclude PAD or determine healing potential in a diabetic foot ulcer.
**Step 5: Foot deformities and joint assessment**
Inspect the foot from above, from the side and from the plantar surface. Ask the patient to move the toes and ankle, and assess gait if safe and appropriate.

items.text: Claw toes or hammer toes.
Hallux valgus.
Prominent metatarsal heads.
Pes cavus or other abnormal arch shape.
Bony prominences.
Previous amputations.
Restricted joint mobility.
Abnormal pressure distribution.
Swelling and changes in foot shape.

blocks.text: Normal: No significant deformity, abnormal prominence, swelling or restricted movement.
Abnormal: Deformities redistribute plantar pressure and increase the risk of callus formation, ulceration and recurrent injury.
**Acute Charcot neuroarthropathy**
This is a particularly important OSCE diagnosis.

Suspect acute Charcot neuroarthropathy in a patient with peripheral neuropathy who develops a hot, red, swollen foot, often with surprisingly little pain. The skin may be intact, and pulses may remain palpable.
It can resemble cellulitis, gout or a deep infection. Charcot neuroarthropathy and infection can also coexist.

items.text: Stop weight-bearing on the affected foot as far as safely possible.
Arrange urgent specialist assessment.
Initiate appropriate immobilisation and offloading under a suitable clinical pathway.
Obtain imaging as indicated; early plain radiographs can be normal.

blocks.text: Do not continue walking the patient around to complete the examination.
**Step 6: Footwear and gait assessment**
Ask the patient to show you their usual shoes and socks, if available.

items.text: Shoes that are too tight or too loose.
Worn or uneven soles.
Seams or objects that could cause friction.
Inadequate toe-box space.
Poor cushioning or inappropriate footwear.
Signs of pressure or friction on the feet.

blocks.text: Ask whether the patient walks barefoot at home or outdoors.
Assess standing and gait only when safe, especially if there is an active ulcer, suspected Charcot foot, severe pain or ischaemia.
Normal: Footwear fits appropriately, provides adequate protection, and does not show obvious pressure-producing defects.
Abnormal: Poorly fitting footwear, recurrent pressure marks and unprotected barefoot walking increase the risk of foot injury.
**Step 7: Additional examination when indicated**
A complete assessment may require examination beyond the feet.

items.text: Lower limbs: Look for oedema, skin changes and other evidence of vascular disease.
Cardiovascular system: Assess relevant cardiovascular risk factors and signs of systemic vascular disease.
Neurological system: Investigate other neurological abnormalities if the pattern is atypical.
General examination: Check for fever, tachycardia, hypotension or systemic toxicity if infection is suspected.

blocks.text: In an ulcerated foot, assess the depth and extent of the wound, the surrounding tissues, possible abscess, tendon or joint involvement, and possible osteomyelitis.

If a wound is infected, classify its severity clinically and arrange appropriate investigations. A superficial swab may reflect colonisation; deep tissue sampling is generally more useful when microbiological sampling is indicated.

subsections.subsection_title: 5. Recognising the main diabetic foot presentations

blocks.text: A. Neuropathic foot
Typically warm, with reduced protective sensation, callus and an ulcer over a pressure point. Pulses may be preserved. The ulcer can be painless.
B. Ischaemic foot
May be cool, pale or cyanosed, with reduced pulses, delayed healing and distal tissue loss. Pain may occur, but neuropathy can mask it.
C. Infected diabetic foot
Look for purulence or inflammatory signs such as swelling, warmth, erythema and tenderness. Assess for deep infection and systemic illness.
D. Charcot foot
A hot, swollen, erythematous foot in a person with neuropathy, sometimes with little pain. Deformity may develop if the condition is not promptly managed.
These patterns are not mutually exclusive. For example, a patient can have neuropathy, PAD and a deep infected ulcer simultaneously.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. How to present your findings to the examiner

blocks.text: This is one of the highest-yield parts of the OSCE. You must distinguish a normal examination from abnormal findings and then state the clinical implications.
“On examination of both feet, the skin is intact, with no ulcers, calluses, fissures, maceration, deformities or signs of infection. The nails and interdigital spaces are unremarkable.
Protective sensation is intact to 10-g monofilament testing at all required sites bilaterally. Vibration sensation is preserved, and ankle reflexes are present.
Both feet are warm, capillary refill is prompt, and the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable bilaterally.
There are no significant foot deformities or abnormal pressure points, and the footwear appears appropriate.
Overall, there are no clinical abnormalities detected on this examination. However, the findings should be interpreted alongside the patient's history and formal diabetic foot risk assessment.”
**Scenario 1: Peripheral neuropathy**
Findings: Reduced monofilament and vibration sensation, with palpable pulses.
Present it like this:

“The patient has reduced protective sensation to monofilament testing and impaired vibration sense bilaterally, with preserved palpable pedal pulses. These findings are consistent with peripheral neuropathy, increasing the risk of unrecognized foot trauma and ulceration.”
Findings: Cool foot, delayed refill, weak pulses and a non-healing ulcer.
Present it like this:

“The affected foot is cool, with delayed capillary refill and diminished dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. There is a non-healing ulcer at the distal foot. These findings raise concern for peripheral arterial disease with impaired tissue perfusion. Urgent vascular assessment is indicated.”
Findings: Plantar ulcer under a metatarsal head, surrounding callus, reduced sensation.
Present it like this:

“There is a plantar ulcer beneath the metatarsal head, surrounded by callus, with reduced protective sensation. Pedal pulses are palpable. The findings suggest a neuropathic pressure ulcer. I would document its dimensions and depth, assess for infection and ischaemia, and arrange appropriate offloading and wound management.”
Findings: Ulcer, purulent discharge, surrounding erythema and swelling.
Present it like this:

“There is an ulcer with purulent discharge, surrounding erythema, warmth and swelling, consistent with a clinically infected diabetic foot ulcer. I would assess the extent and severity of infection, check for systemic involvement, deep tissue infection and ischaemia, and arrange urgent treatment.”
Findings: Black necrotic toe with poor perfusion.
Present it like this:

“There is black necrotic tissue affecting the toe, with clinical evidence of impaired perfusion. This is concerning for gangrene, potentially associated with severe peripheral arterial disease. The patient requires urgent surgical and vascular assessment.”
Findings: Hot, swollen, red foot with neuropathy and relatively little pain.
Present it like this:

“The affected foot is warm, erythematous and swollen in a patient with peripheral neuropathy. Acute Charcot neuroarthropathy is an important differential diagnosis, although infection and other inflammatory conditions must also be considered. I would stop weight-bearing as far as safely possible and arrange urgent specialist assessment.”
Examiners may ask you to classify an ulcer after describing it.
SINBAD is a practical system for describing diabetic foot ulcer severity and supporting communication and audit.

rows: Extends to muscle, tendon or deeper

blocks.text: Each component scores 0 or 1, giving a total from 0 to 6. Higher scores indicate greater overall ulcer severity.
This system combines ulcer depth (grades 0–3) with the presence or absence of infection and ischaemia (stages A–D).

items.text: Grade 0: pre- or post-ulcerative lesion.
Grade 1: superficial wound.
Grade 2: wound extending to tendon or capsule.
Grade 3: wound extending to bone or joint.

blocks.text: Stage A indicates no infection or ischaemia; B indicates infection, C indicates ischaemia, and D indicates both infection and ischaemia.
Another commonly taught system grades ulcers from 0 to 5, from no open ulcer through progressively deeper lesions to extensive gangrene.
Exam tip: Know the principles of each system, but use the classification specifically requested by the examiner or local protocol. These systems do not replace an urgent clinical assessment.
Risk stratification helps determine the need for preventive care and follow-up.

rows: No loss of protective sensation and no PAD
Education, appropriate footwear and regular review
Combinations of neuropathy, PAD or deformity
More frequent review and specialist foot assessment as indicated
Neuropathy or PAD with previous ulcer, amputation or end-stage renal disease, depending on the guideline
High-risk foot care and close surveillance

blocks.text: The exact definitions and follow-up intervals vary by guideline. An active ulcer, infection, gangrene or suspected Charcot foot requires assessment based on the acute problem, not merely assignment to a routine risk category.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Red flags: when the examination becomes urgent

blocks.text: Urgent same-day assessment

items.text: A new hot, red, swollen foot suggesting acute Charcot neuroarthropathy.
A clinically infected diabetic foot ulcer.
Suspected deep infection or osteomyelitis.
New tissue necrosis or gangrene.
A foot ulcer with suspected significant ischaemia.

blocks.text: Emergency assessment

items.text: Sepsis or systemic toxicity.
Wet gangrene or a rapidly spreading infection.
Suspected necrotising infection or deep abscess.
Sudden severe limb ischaemia, especially with a cold, pale foot, new pain, sensory loss or weakness.

blocks.text: Do not wait for fever, severe pain or absent pulses before escalating a concerning diabetic foot presentation. Neuropathy may mask pain, and infection can occur without prominent systemic signs.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Management principles an examiner may ask about

blocks.text: The examination identifies the problem; management depends on the findings.

items.text: Neuropathy without ulceration: Education, daily self-inspection, suitable footwear, professional foot care and periodic risk review.
Callus or pressure lesions: Professional assessment and appropriate pressure reduction; avoid self-cutting or chemical corn treatments in an insensate foot.
Active ulcer: Appropriate wound assessment and care, pressure offloading, evaluation of perfusion, and infection assessment.
Infection: Prompt clinical severity assessment, appropriate antimicrobial treatment when indicated, and drainage or surgical intervention when necessary.
PAD: Objective vascular assessment and specialist referral when indicated; urgent referral for severe ischaemia.
Suspected Charcot foot: Immediate reduction of weight-bearing, appropriate immobilisation and urgent specialist review.

blocks.text: For every patient with diabetes, explain that they should inspect their feet daily, avoid walking barefoot, check the inside of their shoes, wash and dry their feet carefully (especially between the toes), moisturise dry skin without applying moisturiser between the toes, and seek prompt review for any new wound, blister, swelling or colour change.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. Why is the 10-g monofilament important?
It assesses protective pressure sensation and helps identify patients at risk of foot ulceration due to loss of protective sensation.
Q2. Can a patient with palpable pedal pulses still have PAD?
Yes. Palpable pulses do not exclude PAD. Objective vascular assessment may be necessary if symptoms, ulcers or other findings raise suspicion.
Q3. Why can an ABPI be misleading in diabetes?
Medial arterial calcification may make the arteries poorly compressible, resulting in a falsely elevated or apparently normal ABPI.
Q4. Why are diabetic foot ulcers often painless?
Peripheral sensory neuropathy can reduce the perception of pain, pressure and injury.
Q5. What is the difference between a neuropathic and an ischaemic ulcer?

Neuropathic ulcers often occur at plantar pressure points with callus and reduced sensation. Ischaemic ulcers more often affect distal or marginal areas and are associated with impaired perfusion. Mixed ulcers are common.
Q6. What are the classic signs of infection?
Purulence or local inflammatory findings such as redness, warmth, swelling and tenderness. Assess the extent of infection and look for systemic involvement.
Q7. What should you suspect in a hot, swollen diabetic foot with little pain?
Acute Charcot neuroarthropathy is a key diagnosis, although infection and other causes must be considered.
Q8. What is the most important previous history to establish?
Previous ulceration or amputation, because either identifies a patient at particularly high risk of future foot complications.
Q9. What is the most important action if gangrene is found?
Urgent assessment by the appropriate surgical and vascular teams, with emergency treatment when infection, wet gangrene or acute ischaemia is suspected.

items.text: Examining only the dorsum and forgetting the sole, heel and interdigital spaces.
Forgetting to examine both feet.
Failing to test protective sensation properly.
Palpating only one pedal pulse.
Treating capillary refill as a definitive test of circulation.
Assuming that an ulcer without pain is harmless.
Failing to document ulcer size, site, depth and infection signs.
Missing a hot, swollen foot suggestive of Charcot neuroarthropathy.
Forgetting footwear assessment and previous ulcer history.
Failing to state the urgency of the findings.

blocks.text: Use this checklist to practise the station.
0 of 12 completed
Introduce yourself, obtain consent and position the patient appropriately
Ask about diabetes duration, symptoms, previous ulcers and amputations
Inspect both feet, including soles, heels, nails and interdigital spaces
Describe any ulcer by site, size, depth, wound bed and infection signs
Test 10-g monofilament sensation at the required sites
Assess vibration sensation and ankle reflexes
Compare temperature and assess capillary refill
Palpate dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally
Inspect deformities, calluses, pressure points and previous amputations
Assess footwear and gait if safe
Identify urgent red flags and state the next step
Summarise normal or abnormal findings clearly to the examiner
If the examiner asks you to summarise the whole examination in 20–30 seconds, use this structure:

“I examined both feet for skin integrity, ulcers, infection, deformities, protective sensation and vascular sufficiency. My main findings are [state abnormalities]. These suggest [clinical interpretation]. I would assess the patient's overall ulcer risk and, if indicated, arrange urgent wound, vascular or specialist assessment.”

Remember: in a diabetic foot station, the three things you must never miss are loss of protective sensation, impaired arterial perfusion and infection. A hot, swollen foot also requires you to consider acute Charcot neuroarthropathy.
